la:verb:queo.html:
quĕo, īvi and ii, ĭtum, v. n.
etym. dub.; cf. Sanscr. ?*!vay āmi, am strong or able
,
to be able, I (thou, he, etc.) can (class.; esp. freq. with a negation; Cic. does not use nequeo in the first pers. sing.; for a full account of the forms in use, v. Neue, Formenl. 2, p. 607 sqq.; cf.: possum, polleo, valeo).—With inf.: non queo reliqua scribere,: non quis,: non quit sentire dolorem,: ut quimus,: quod vos dicere non quitis,: quod manu non queunt tangere,: queam,; : queas,; : queat,: queamus,: si queant,: non quibam,: quibat,; : quirem,: quiret,; : quirent,: nec credere quivi,: quivit,; : quiit, Att. ap. : quivimus,: quistis,: quiverunt, Quadrig. ap. : quivere,: quivero,: quiverit,; : quierit,: quiveritis,: quiverint,: quissent,: quibo,: quibunt,: quiens,; in abl.: queunte,: quire,: quisse,.— Affirmatively: hoc queo dicere,: habere quod queant dicere,; : queat,: queamus,: queunt,; . — In pass.: si non sarciri quitur, Caecil. ap. P.: percipi queuntur, Att. ib.: suppleri queatur,: subigi queantur,: neque vi impelli, neque prece quitus sum, could not be driven, Att. ap. P.: forma nosci non quita est,.—As dep.: pollicitus ita facturum, ne sic quidem quitus est,could not, was not able,.

la:noun:querela.html:
quĕrēla or quĕrella, ae, f.
queror
,
a complaining, complaint (class.).
Lit.
Ingen.: intervenit nonnullorum querelis,: hominum vel admiratio vel querela,: inveterata,: epistula plena querelarum,: longae,: vestrum beneficium nonnullam habet querelam,gives some occasion for complaint,: his de tot tantisque injuriis,: cui sunt inauditae cum Deiotaro querelae tuae?: querela Lucretiae patris ac propinquorum,: QVI VIXIT SINE VLLA QVERELA CVM CONIVGE,without any complaint,.—With obj.-gen.: frontis tui,: querela temporum,against the times,: aequalium meorum,.— With quod: an quod a sociis eorum non abstinuerim, justam querelam habent,.—With obj.clause: falsa est querela, paucissimis hominibus vim percipiendi, quae tradantur, esse concessam,. —
In partic., a complaint, accusation (postAug.): advocati flagitabant, uti judex querelam inspiceret,: frequentes,: instituere,to institute,; ; . —
Transf.
A plaintive song for lulling children to sleep: longa somnum suadere querela,. —
A plaintive sound, plaintive note, plaint; of animals or instruments. — Of swans: tollunt lugubri voce querellam,.— Of frogs: et veterem in limo ranae cecinere querellam,; cf. .—Of doves, .— Of the plaintive tones of the tibia: dulcesque querellas, Tibia quas fundit,; .—
A pain that occasions complaining, a complaint, disease, malady: pulmonis ac viscerum querelas levare,; Traj. ap. (29), 1.

la:conj:que.html:
quĕ (lengthened in arsis by the poets, like the Gr. τε:
Faunique Satyrique,; ; ; ), conj. enclitic [kindr. with Gr. τε, κε, and Sanscr. ca, the same], a copulative particle affixed to the word it annexes. According to Dräger (Hist. Synt. Th. 3, p. 32), it is, in archaic and official language, preferred to et, from which it is distinguished by denoting a closer connection. It is used,
Singly, to effect,
Co-ordination of words,
Of cognate meaning: fames sitisque,: augeri amplificarique,: admirabilis incredibilisque,: fuga pavorque,: cibus victusque,: concilium coetusque,: res rationesque,: blandimenta voluptatis otiique,: extremum summumque supplicium,: imperio auspicioque,: carus acceptusque,: jus fasque,. — Esp. in phrases like longe longeque,; : longe multumque,: saepe diuque,. — With comp.: plus plusque,: magis magisque,: minus minusque,; with personal and possessive pronouns: me meosque,: ipse meique,; and in archaic formulae: potes pollesque,: vivunt vigentque,. —
Of contrasted meaning: jus nefasque,: longe lateque, Naev. ap. : cominus eminusque,: ultro citroque,: terrā marique,: ferro ignique,: pace belloque,: belli domique,: domi ferisque,: tempus locusque,: parvis magnisque,: floribus coronisque,flowers loose and bound up,. —
Adding a detail or explanation (not in Cic.).
General: fratres consanguineosque,: largitiones temeritatisque invitamenta,: ad tempus non venit, metusque rem impediebat,: a fallaci equitum specie agasonibusque,: Graeco peregrinoque sermone, Just. praef. 1. —
Special to general: arma tantum ferrumque in dextris,. —
General to special: nostra consilia quaeque in castris gerantur,: obsides daturos quaeque imperasset facturos,: regno fortunisque omnibus expulit,: Baliares levemque armaturam,.—
Introducing an explanatory clause, and so (Liv.): fretusque his animis Aeneas,: Sabinusque,. —
In an answer (very rare): Ain heri nos adventisse huc? Aio, adveniensque ilico me salutasti,.—
Equivalent to quoque only in hodieque (not before Velleius): quae hodieque appellatur Ionia,: quae hodieque celebres sunt,: in Abydi gymnasio colitur hodieque,: et hodieque reliquiae durant,: sunt clari hodieque,. —
Connecting final member of a clause: fauste, feliciter, prospereque,: ab honore, famā fortunisque,fin.: pacem, tranquillitatem, otium concordiamque afferat,. —
In transition to a new subject or thought: quoniamque ea natura esset hominis,: discriptioque sacerdotum nullum justae religionis genus praetermittit,; v. Madv. ad. .—
Repeated, que . . . que.
Both ... and (not in Cæs., once in Cic.; v. Zumpt, Gram. § 338), co-ordinating,
Similar notions: quasque incepistis res, quasque inceptabitis,: risusque jocosque,.—
Contrasted notions: meque teque,: mores veteresque novosque tenentem, Enn. ap. Gell. 12, 4, 4: mittuntque feruntque,: noctesque diesque,.—
Esp. when one or both of the words are pronouns: seque remque publicam curabant,: quique in urbe erant, quosque acciverant,: quique exissent, quique ibi mansissent,.—
Que ... que, and ... and, the first que referring to a previous clause: singulasque res definimus, circumscripteque

complectimur, .—

More than twice.
Que ... que ... que: quod mihique eraeque filiaeque erili est,: regnaque tristia, Divosque mortalesque turbas regit,.—
Four times, ; five times,; seven times,.—
Followed by other conjunctions.
Que ... et (not in Cic., Cæs., Suet., or Nep.): peregrique et domi,: deus, qui quae nos gerimus auditque et videt,: seque et oppidum tradat,: illosque et Sullam,: signaque et ordines,; Weissenb. ad loc.: legatique et tribuni,: in formulam jurisque et dicionis,: omnes gentesque et terrae, (v. Fabri ad loc.): Arpinique et Romani,: seque et arma,: seque et delatores,.—
Que ... et ... et: Romanique et Macedones et socii,: seque et arma et equos,: seque et domum et pacem,; . —
Que ... ac (rare, not earlier than Verg.): satisque ac super,: minusque ac minus,: oculisque ac mente turbatus,: posuitque domos atque horrea fecit,: seque ac liberos suos,: opibusque atque honoribus,. —
Que ... ac ... et: in quos seque ac conjuges et liberos condunt,. —
Que ... et ... ac, . —
Following a conjunction, et ... que: paratissimi et ab exercitu reliquisque rebus, Brut. ap. , a, 5: id et singulis universisque honori fuisse, (Weissenb. et id); occasionally in Cic. (through negligence, acc. to Madvig): igitur et Epaminondas ... Themistoclesque,: officia et servata praetermissaque,.—
Que nearly equivalent to autem, sed ..., but (not in Cæs.): studio ad rempublicam latus sum ibique multa mihi advorsa fuere,but there,.—Mostly after a negative: Socrates nec patronum quaesivit nec judicibus supplex fuit, adhibuitque liberam contumaciam,; : qui non temere movendam rem tantam expectandosque ex Hispaniā legatos censerent,: quae neque dant flammas lenique vapore cremantur,.—
Que is usually appended to the first word of the phrase, but to a noun rather than to a monosyllabic preposition governing it, unless the preposition is repeated: de provinciāque,: per vimque,; cf.: ab iisque,: sub occasumque solis,.— Exceptions are to be found, especially in Liv.: proque ignoto,: exque eo tempore,; : inque eam rem,: inque eo exercitu,: inque eam rem,; ; ; : cumque eis,: proque,; ; : deque praedā,: perque,; ; : transque,: aque,: eque,; : exque eo,: perque somnum,.—And where the same preposition is repeated que is regularly joined to it: haec de se, deque provinciā,; ; ; 31, 5, 4; 38, 35, 7: de matrimonio Agrippinae, deque Neronis adoptione,: per senectutem tuam, perque eam, quam, etc.,. — Where the preposition is dissyllabic it regularly takes the que: interque eos,; : sine scutis sineque ferro,. — It is rarely annexed to the second word of the clause, when the first word is an adverb: tantos tam praecipitisque casus,: tanto tam immensoque campo, al.—In class. Latin que is not appended to hic, sic, nunc, huc, etc. (v. Madv. ad. ): hucque et illuc,; : tuncque (1); 14, 15.—Que is often misplaced by the poets, especially by Tibullus and Propertius in the latter part of the pentameter: Messallam terrā dum sequiturque mari,: ferratam Danaes transiliamque domum,.

la:verb:queror.html:
quĕror, questus, 3,
v. dep. a. and n.
Sanscr. root, c?*!vas-, to sigh
.
Lit.
In gen., to complain, lament, bewail (class.).
With acc.: suas fortunas, to bewail one's fate, : suum fatum,: injuriam,: omnia,: fortunam,: nova monstra,: labem atque ignominiam rei publicae,.—
With de: queritur de Milone per vim expulso,: de injuriis alicujus,.—
With cum: quererer tecum, atque expostularem, ni,I would complain to you,: cum patribus conscriptis,: cum deo, quod,; : tecum inconsideratae pietatis queror,.—
With apud: apud novercam,: apud aliquem per litteras,.— (ε) With dat.: nec quereris patri?nor complain to your father?.— (ζ) With obj.-clause: ne querantur se relictas esse,.—(η) With quod: legatos miserunt Athenas questum, quod, etc.,: queri libet, quod in secreta nostra non inquirant principes,; cf.: quereris super hoc, quod non mittam carmina,. —(θ) With pro: haec pro re publicā,in behalf of, in the name of the State,.— (ι) Absol.: nisi omni tempore, quod mihi lege concessum est, abusus ero, querere,: non injuste,.—
In partic., to make a complaint before a court: de proconsulatu alicujus,.—
Transf., of animals and things that utter a plaintive sound. Of apes: queri rauco stridore,.— Of the owl,. — In gen., of the song of birds,to complain, lament, to coo, warble, sing,: dulce queruntur aves,.—Of a musical instrument: flebile nescio quid queritur lyra,; .

la:noun:quercus.html:
quercus, ūs (
gen. querci, ; gen. plur. quercorum, ap. P.; dat. and abl. plur. do not occur), f.
perh. from root kar (kal-k), to be hard; cf.: cornu calx, calculus
.
An oak, oaktree, esp. the Italian or esculent oak, sacred to Jupiter (cf. robur): quercus dicitur, quod id genus arboris grave sit ac durum, tum etiam in ingentem evadat amplitudinem: querqueram enim gravem et magnam putant dici, Paul. ex Müll.: percellunt magnas quercus, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 194 Vahl.): magna Jovis quercus,: glandiferae,; : aëriae,: quercus et ilex Multā fruge pecus juvat,: auritae,: aridae,: durior annosā quercu,: quercorum rami, ap. P.—
Poet., transf.
?*!f things made of oak-wood. Of a ship, of the ship Argo, .— Of a javelin, .— Of a drinkingvessel, .— Capitolina,a garland of oak-leaves,; usually bestowed upon one who had saved the life of a citizen in battle,; ; : civilis,. —
For acorns (very rare): veteris fastidia quercūs,.

questus, ūs, m.

la:adv:quemadmodum.html:
quĕmadmŏdum or quĕm ad mŏ-dum, adv.,
in what manner, how (cf.: quomodo, quī).
Interrog.: facere amicum tibi me potis es sempiternum. Sa. Quemadmodum? : si non reliquit: quemadmodum ab eo postea exegisti?: quem ad modum est adservatus?; ; . —
Rel.: ego omnem rem scio, quemadmodum est,: semper vigilavi, et providi, quemadmodum salvi esse possemus,; ; ; ; ; .—
In partic.
Corresp. with sic, ita, etc., just as, as: quemadmodum urbes magnas viculis praeferundas puto, sic, etc.,; cf.: si, quemadmodum soles de ceteris rebus ... sic de amicitiā disputaris,. — Corresp. with ita, , a, 4; ; with item, ; with eodem modo, ; with adaeque,.—
In introducing examples, as, as for instance: quemadmodum C. Caesar inquit,; ; ; 9, 2, 36 al.: quemadmodum si,.
